extracted.intended_audience: political science researchers, administrative law scholars, and graduate students studying rulemaking and public participation
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, definitions, and coding instructions for analyzing public pressure campaigns and public comments in U.S. federal agency rulemaking, including definitions of coalitions, mobilization, information types, and operational measures of influence and responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coalition
rubrics_metrics.description: A coalition is a group of people and organizations pursuing the same aims in the same policy fight. Because coordination is difficult to measure, the empirical definition includes individuals and organizations who advocate for the same policy outcomes regardless of overt coordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A coalition may include organizations lobbying for the same policy outcome for different reasons (e.g., 'bootleggers and baptists' coalitions). Use textual and positional similarity across comments to identify coalition membership when overt coordination is not observable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Going public
rubrics_metrics.description: Going public describes the choice to pursue an 'outside' strategy to influence policy outcomes. It aims to expand the scope of conflict and involve more actors than would be involved when lobbying organizations only employ an 'inside' lobbying strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast going-public campaigns (mobilizing citizens, mass commenting, public events) with inside lobbying (professional policy influencers). Treat campaigns that recruit public participation as attempts to change the political information environment around a rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grassroots and astroturf campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Grassroots campaigns aim to mobilize individuals based on some pre-existing interest or belief. In contrast, astroturf campaigns aim to create a deceptive appearance of more public support; organizers may be paying participants or using misleading information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Astroturf may involve deceived or financially incentivized participants or fake/non-consenting names; grassroots campaigns may still use simplification, spin, or funding, but do so without quid pro quo. Distinguish these types when possible, but note that both are 'outside' lobbying strategies and can be empirically similar in comment text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lobbying influence (causal implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lobbying influence implies a causal effect between an effort to influence policy and a policy outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use causal inference strategies when claiming influence; avoid equating observed association (e.g., many comments and a policy change) with causal influence without identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lobbying success (outcome without causal claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lobbying success describes a situation where a group that sought to influence policy got the outcome they sought, without implying a causal relationship between their effort and the policy outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize success as whether the desired policy outcome occurred (e.g., language added/removed, regulatory stringency changed) but separate this measurement from causal claims about the campaign's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership organization
rubrics_metrics.description: A membership organization is a type of organization formed to serve the interests of a defined membership; may act in the name of members' narrow material interests or broader visions of the public interest. Some membership organizations are more directly governed by their members than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding comments, note whether a comment claims to represent a membership organization and consider governance differences as contextual information about representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobilizing groups/organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mobilizing groups/organizations recruit people to take an action (e.g., to sign a petition or submit a public comment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify mobilizing actors by linking comment metadata (uploader, batch uploads) and matching text patterns to known mobilizers. Separate organization-uploaded comments from individual submissions when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization (comment authorship rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization is usually incorporated as a business, government, or non-profit. Public comments from organizations represent the position of the organization as an incorporated entity only if the comment text claims to represent the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not count an employee using letterhead as an organizational comment unless the text claims organizational representation. Letters from elected officials count as representing their governmental organization only if they explicitly claim to do so and are in a position to do so (e.g., governor or committee chair); otherwise count them as individual politicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest group
rubrics_metrics.description: A public interest group is a type of organization that primarily advocates for some vision of the public good, not the private material interest of its owners or members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify organizations' type (public interest, business, membership) as part of coalition and mobilization analyses; multiple public interest groups may form competing coalitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public pressure campaign
rubrics_metrics.description: A public pressure campaign is an effort to influence policy by mobilizing a segment of the public to pay attention to the policy process and express their opinions to decisionmakers. It can be an astroturf or grassroots campaign on behalf of public or private interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirically focus on campaigns targeting public comment periods (mass commenting campaigns). Distinguish campaigns by organizer, scale, whether comments are form letters, and whether comments were uploaded in batches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass comment (operational definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: For analytic purposes, a mass comment is defined as any comment sharing a substantial amount of text with 99 other comments or uploaded in a batch of 100 or more by the same organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use text matching and batch-upload metadata to label comments as 'mass comments.' This threshold operationalizes mass mobilization for the dataset and analyses in the dissertation; adjust threshold transparently if used in other contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsiveness is observable attention that government officials pay to public input. This can be either substantive policy influence or discursive influence (procedural responsiveness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure responsiveness via changes in rule text between draft and final rules, explicit agency responses to comments, congressional oversight actions triggered by campaigns, or inclusion of issues (e.g., environmental justice) in final documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical information
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical information includes scientific or legal facts. It may influence decisions if policymakers update their beliefs about the consequences of their policy—for example, by changing an economic cost-benefit analysis or by revealing an unknown legal precedent or statutory requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding comment content, flag statements that provide empirical evidence, legal citations, citations to studies, or domain-specific facts as technical information. Consider whether agencies used or cited that technical information in responses or final rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political information
rubrics_metrics.description: Political information is about the political context in which policy is made. It may influence decisions if policymakers update their beliefs about which members of Congress support their proposal, the prevalence of a belief in the broader public, or the number of people an interest group represents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code comments or campaign artifacts that provide electoral information, threats of oversight, measures of public opinion, or demonstrations of constituent counts as political information. Recognize many political information signals are second-order beliefs (beliefs about what others think).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructions for coding comment position (A.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A.1 provides instructions for coding the position of a comment given current policy, X1, and proposed policy, X2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code a comment's spatial position relative to policy change (support, oppose, neutral, or position regarding direction/degree of change) using explicit rules that compare X1 and X2. Use examples and decision rules in A.1 to ensure consistent positional coding across coders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding responses to comments (A.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A.2 describes coding procedures for agency responses to comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing responsiveness and discursive influence, code whether and how agency responses address specific comment claims (technical or political), whether they change reasoning or rule text, and whether they cite particular comments or organized coalitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding rules and coder instructions (A.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A.3 contains the coding rules used throughout the hand-coded datasets (rules for coding comments, responses, and related variables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow A.3 for consistent variable definitions, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and handling edge cases (e.g., ambiguous authorship, duplicated text, batch uploads). Use codebook examples and protocols to resolve ambiguous cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying mobilizing coalitions by matching text
rubrics_metrics.description: Coalitions can be identified by the percent of matching text in a sample of public comments (used to detect form letters and mass-mobilized campaigns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute pairwise text-matching shares or clustering of comment text to detect groups of highly similar comments; set thresholds (e.g., 'substantial amount of text') consistent with the mass comment operational definition and report sensitivity checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding spatial position of comments on proposed policy changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Coding the spatial position of comments involves mapping comment content to positions on the proposed change (e.g., support/oppose, direction and magnitude relative to X1 and X2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the decision tree in A.1 and examples in the codebook to place comments on a spatial scale; record uncertainty and inter-coder reliability statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalizing lobbying success in empirical models
rubrics_metrics.description: Lobbying success is operationalized at coalition and organization levels (e.g., whether the outcome sought was achieved) and modeled using OLS, mediation analysis, and difference-in-difference approaches to assess associations with campaign characteristics and congressional support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish descriptive measures of success from causal identification. Include control variables and consider mediation by congressional support; use robustness checks and alternative model specifications as illustrated in Chapter 3 (OLS models, mediation analysis, difference-in-difference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring changes in rule text (environmental justice example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure whether specific concepts (e.g., 'environmental justice') are added between draft and final rules; predict changes using logit regression and examine probabilities by president, number of comments, and agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize textual change as the explicit addition (or removal) of target language between drafts and finals. Use hand-coded indicators or text-difference algorithms; model with appropriate covariates and present predicted probabilities and marginal effects (Ch.4 approach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying mobilizing organizations and scale of campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify organizations that mobilize comments (e.g., organizations mobilizing the most public comments 2005–2020) and measure the frequency and scale of public pressure campaigns by coalition type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metadata (uploader, batch uploads), text-matching, and organizational registries to attribute mobilized comments to organizations. Report counts, distributions over agencies and time, and breakdowns by coalition types (public vs private).
